Compared masking.py:63-124 with issue-context.md lines 35-37. split_label_words splits on non-alnum chars (99-112). _split_chunk (71-96) groups chars into U/L/D runs, which gives lower-to-upper boundaries and letter/digit boundaries. For a U run followed by an L run it splits before the last capital (89-91), so APIKey gives api, key. The acronym exception (86-87) keeps a single 's' when the L run is exactly 's' and it is at the chunk end (end of label or before a non-alnum char) or before a digit. This matches 'end of label or before a non-letter', so PINs gives pins, and PINs2 and PINs_x also keep the s. password2 gives password, 2. Words are lowercased. _word_matches (115-116) accepts only equality, +s or +es, as the rule states. _label_matches (119-124) requires consecutive in-order words. Configured entries use the same split_label_words (137). I found no counterexample.

factory.py:214-268 build_sql_runner has keyword read_only: bool = True and passes read_only through to PostgresRunner (247-252) and MySQLRunner (257-268). Postgres sql_runner.py:147 calls conn.set_session(readonly=True) only if self._read_only, so read_only=False skips it. Non-read-shaped statements run via a plain cursor and conn.commit() (199-209). MySQL sql_runner.py:120-126 issues SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY only if self._read_only, and non-read statements commit (155-159). Both runners are therefore writable at read_only=False. Column labels: Postgres uses RealDictCursor (179) and MySQL uses SSDictCursor (149), so the DataFrame columns are the driver's result-column names, bare names (id, password_hash) for SELECT * on a simple table. The test at tests/connectors/test_connectors.py:135-153 relies on exactly this. I did not run it against live databases. The bare-name label comes from reading the driver cursor behaviour, not from executing anything.
